_metadata.independence: I read only the brief and the single input file x20-rb-input.json; no other repository files, searches, web or paid APIs were used.

hints.reason: Clean double meaning: gin the spirit for ALCOHOL and the cotton gin machine for COTTON, both familiar from school and the bar.

pairs.pair_note: Textbook double meaning; keep as is.

hints.reason: Springsteen is 'The Boss' for BOSS and the voice of 'Born in the U.S.A.' and heartland Americana for AMERICA; both routes are well known.

pairs.pair_note: Strong classic-rock aha; nickname side is the click.

hints.reason: Arrow shaft (the body of the arrow) for ARROW and mine shaft (the tunnel down) for MINE; two real senses of one word.

pairs.pair_note: Solid, fair double meaning.

hints.reason: Styx the classic rock band ('Come Sail Away') for BAND and the mythic river of the underworld for RIVER; a satisfying two-world link.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; classic-rock reference is fine for the audience.

hints.reason: AQUA means water (Latin, and aqua color) for WATER, and Aqua is the band behind the hugely familiar 'Barbie Girl' for BARBIE; a real 'oh, nice' moment.

pairs.pair_note: One of the best in the batch; the band name is less known than the song, but the explanation clicks instantly.

hints.reason: The tornado that carries Dorothy to Oz is iconic for TORNADO; Toto riding in Dorothy's basket is a well-remembered film image for BASKET, if a softer second step.

pairs.pair_note: Basket side is the weaker half but is a true, memorable film detail.

hints.reason: The Princess and the Pea (a pea under the mattresses) for BED and split pea soup for SOUP; fairy tale plus kitchen gives a nice aha.

pairs.pair_note: Charming; the fairy-tale side is the payoff.

hints.reason: Fangs are the teeth you bite with for BITE and the signature vampire feature for VAMPIRE; obvious but honest and clear.

pairs.pair_note: Easy, clear clue; low delight is not a reason to fail.

hints.reason: 'Heavenly body' is an instantly familiar phrase for BODY, and a planet is a classic heavenly body for PLANET; one phrase covers both, but it lands.
hints.fix: PLANET line: "Planets and stars have long been called heavenly bodies." (astronomers' usual term is 'celestial bodies').

pairs.pair_note: Phrase-join that works because the phrase is the very definition of a planet; small text fix only.

hints.reason: A car's trunk for CAR, and the familiar British 'boot' meaning the trunk for BOOT; the British sense is widely known to U.S. players.

pairs.pair_note: Matches the owner's own example of an acceptable British word; note TRUNK also appears as a target on the EAR/TRUNK pair, so avoid both on one board.

hints.reason: The Wright brothers for BROTHER, and the aviation pioneers who flew their own plane in 1903 for PILOT; both sides click at once.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent history hint; the homophone 'right' adds a little misdirection.

hints.reason: Bugs Bunny supplies BUG through his name and CARROT through his signature carrot-munching; the cartoon makes it instant.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; BUNNY brings rabbit-and-carrot to mind even before the cartoon, which helps.

hints.reason: Camp David, the presidential retreat, for CAMP and David who slew the giant Goliath for GIANT; two unrelated Davids make a real aha.

pairs.pair_note: Top-tier: history plus Bible story through one name.

hints.reason: A lap around the track for TRACK and the lap a cat curls up on (cats also lap milk) for CAT; tidy double meaning.

pairs.pair_note: Lap-cat plus lapping milk gives the CAT side two routes.

hints.reason: A rabbit's foot for RABBIT, which is the classic lucky charm for CHARM; one object, but both words come to mind quickly.

pairs.pair_note: Fair and easy; LUCKY would point at CHARM more than RABBIT, so FOOT is the right pick.

hints.reason: The phone-booth costume change is iconic for PHONE; the S shield on his chest (and the shirt-ripping reveal) gives CHEST, a softer but true second step.

pairs.pair_note: Chest side may take a beat; it clicks once you picture the S. Second opinion welcome on whether CHEST is reached without the explanation.

hints.reason: A pew is a church bench for CHURCH and 'pew pew' is the playful laser-blast sound for LASER; funny, fair and clever.

pairs.pair_note: A favourite: playful sound-effect sense paired with a solemn one.

hints.reason: Mouseketeers were the cast of The Mickey Mouse Club for CLUB and wore the famous mouse-ear hats for EAR; both are core to the image.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pop-culture hint; the ears hat is iconic.

hints.reason: DC Comics for COMIC and Washington, D.C. for WASHINGTON; short, instantly recognizable double reference.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; compact and fair.

hints.reason: Thin Mints give THIN by name and COOKIE as the famous Girl Scout cookie; one product name covers both cleanly.

pairs.pair_note: Easy but satisfying brand clue.

hints.reason: A plaintiff files a (law)suit for SUIT and brings the case to court for COURT; the legal sense of SUIT is the small aha.

pairs.pair_note: Clear legal-sense link; LAWSUIT-adjacent hints like LAW would be phrase-joins and no better.

hints.reason: The crash cymbal for CRASH and the cymbals that sit in every typical drum kit for DRUM; easy and true.

pairs.pair_note: Plain but sound; possible homophone confusion with 'symbol' adds mild fun.

hints.reason: 'Due date' for DATE, and library books being due back for LIBRARY; a familiar phrase plus a familiar everyday fact.

pairs.pair_note: Instantly familiar phrase-join; the library side gives it a second real anchor.

hints.reason: Tart the pastry for DESSERT and tart the sour taste for LEMON (with lemon tart tying them together); neat double meaning.

pairs.pair_note: Very good; noun and adjective senses both land.

hints.reason: 'The dog days of summer' completes both DOG and SUMMER in one instantly familiar idiom; the Sirius line adds a real fact.

pairs.pair_note: Phrase-join that passes because the idiom is universal; DAYS alone is broad, so board context matters.

hints.reason: Dumbo's giant flying ears are iconic for EAR; TRUNK comes from his being an elephant, which is generic but true and quickly reached.

pairs.pair_note: Better than plain ELEPHANT because the ears are the point of Dumbo; trunk side is the softer half.

hints.reason: 'I am your father' for FATHER and the dark side of the Force for FORCE; one of the most famous movie reveals.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent and broad.

hints.reason: Snapping your fingers for FINGER and Snap of Snap, Crackle and Pop, the Rice Krispies elves, for RICE; cereal-mascot aha.

pairs.pair_note: A favourite; the cereal mascot is the payoff.

hints.reason: The Venus flytrap for FLY and Venus the second planet for PLANET; science plus botany through one name.

pairs.pair_note: Strong and fair.

hints.reason: Hercules (Greek Heracles) is the archetypal hero of Greek myth, giving GREECE and HERO together; Disney's 'Zero to Hero' reinforces it.

pairs.pair_note: Explanation correctly handles the Roman/Greek name; easy, satisfying.

hints.reason: 'High roller' (big gambler) for HIGH and 'roller skate' for SKATE; both compounds are instantly familiar and use different senses.

pairs.pair_note: Clean two-compound join; passes on familiarity.

hints.reason: INTERNET is reached via clickbait/rage bait and TROLL via 'don't take the bait' or the fishing sense of trolling, but both routes lean on the single phrase 'internet troll' and the fishing sense is not widely known.

pairs.pair_note: True but murky; FEED ('don't feed the trolls' plus your internet feed) gives two cleaner, more familiar routes. INTERNET line could lean on clickbait rather than trolls.

hints.reason: A leaf is a page of a book ('leaf through') for LEAF, and a page was the boy who trained toward knighthood (page, squire, knight) for KNIGHT; a satisfying indirect aha.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent owner-style indirect knowledge; page-to-knight ladder is familiar from school history.

hints.reason: 'Turn over a new leaf' supplies both TURN and LEAF in one universally known idiom; NEW is generic but the idiom snaps into place.

pairs.pair_note: Acceptable phrase-join on an instantly familiar idiom; LEAF also appears in the KNIGHT/LEAF pair, so keep them off one board.

hints.reason: A silver medal (second place) for MEDAL and the silver screen (the movies) for SCREEN; two distinct, familiar senses.

pairs.pair_note: Classic and pleasing.

hints.reason: Corona, the Mexican beer, for MEXICO and the solar corona seen during eclipses for SUN; brand plus astronomy is a nice aha.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; a beer brand is PG enough given GIN is also in the batch.

hints.reason: A vanity mirror (and the vanity table it sits on) for MIRROR and a vanity license plate for PLATE; both are everyday terms and the pairing is clever.

pairs.pair_note: Very good; vanity = self-regard ties the two together thematically too.

hints.reason: Many U.S. players know Naruto is an anime ninja (NINJA), but his love of ramen (NOODLE) is fan-level detail; the narutomaki fish-cake ramen topping is a real backup that most players also will not know.

pairs.pair_note: Close to the rejected anime-trivia line on the noodle side; the explanation could mention the naruto fish cake in ramen to strengthen it.

hints.reason: Sgt. Pepper of the Beatles album for PEPPER and the military rank staff sergeant for STAFF; music plus military makes a satisfying click.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; also evokes Dr Pepper as misdirection.

hints.reason: Both sides go through the setting of Plants vs. Zombies (plant defenders on your lawn, zombies crossing it); PLANT is loosely reachable via gardening, but ZOMBIE needs the game detail, so most players see it only after the explanation.

pairs.pair_note: The targets are the game title itself, so the hint has to be a game detail; LAWN is true but indirect. No clearly better single word found.

hints.reason: 'Video Killed the Radio Star' contains both RADIO and STAR in a title nearly everyone knows; the first-MTV-video fact is a fun, true bonus.

pairs.pair_note: Title-based phrase-join that earns its pass through instant familiarity.

hints.reason: A hermit lives a solitary life for SOLITARY and hermit crabs live in borrowed shells for SHELL; the near-synonym is fine because the crab gives a real second link.

pairs.pair_note: Lovely nature-plus-word-sense pairing.

hints.reason: 'Slow as molasses' for SLOW and molasses as the syrup left from sugar-making for SUGAR; saying plus kitchen fact.

pairs.pair_note: Sound; the sugar side is a real fact many cooks know.

hints.reason: METRO is a common word for a subway for SUBWAY, and Washington, D.C.'s system is famously called the Metro for WASHINGTON; the D.C. side is a real but softer link.

pairs.pair_note: Washington side is the weak half since many cities have a Metro; D.C.'s is the best-known U.S. one, so it holds. Second opinion welcome.
